[2024 fall ms applied — problem 4]

Multiple regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, X_3$, $n = 25$, SS(Total) $= 248.0$; table of SSReg for all predictor subsets (SSReg($X_1,X_2,X_3) = 181.8$, SSReg($X_1,X_2) = 145.2$, etc.), $\alpha = 0.05$. (1) Global F-test of $H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0$. (2) Compute the extra SSReg$(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)$. (3) Test whether $X_3$ can be dropped. (4) Write the first row of the reduced-model $X$-matrix testing $H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_3 = 0$ (first obs: $Y=10, X_1=1985, X_2=59.7, X_3=2205$).

## Part (1): Global F-test

**Hypotheses:** $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = 0$ vs $H_a:$ at least one $\beta_j \neq 0$

**Test statistic:**
$$F = \frac{\text{SSReg}/(p)}{SS(Residual)/(n-p-1)}$$

where $p = 3$ (number of predictors)

$SS(Residual) = SS(Total) - SSReg(X_1, X_2, X_3) = 248.0 - 181.8 = 66.2$


$$F = \frac{181.8/3}{66.2/21} = \frac{60.6}{3.1524} \approx 19.21$$

With $df_1 = 3$ and $df_2 = 21$, the critical value is $F_{0.05}(3, 21) \approx 3.07$. Since $F = 19.21 > 3.07$, I reject $H_0$, indicating at least one predictor contributes significantly to the model.

## Part (2): Extra SSReg$(X_3 | X_1, X_2)$

The partial regression sum of squares measures the additional contribution of $X_3$ after accounting for $X_1$ and $X_2$:
$$\text{SSReg}(X_3 | X_1, X_2) = \text{SSReg}(X_1, X_2, X_3) - \text{SSReg}(X_1, X_2)$$
$$= 181.8 - 145.2 = 36.6$$

## Part (3): Test whether $X_3$ can be dropped

Testing $H_0: \beta_3 = 0$ against $H_a: \beta_3 \neq 0$, the test statistic is:
$$F = \frac{36.6}{3.1524} \approx 11.60$$

With critical value $F_{0.05}(1, 21) \approx 4.32$, since $11.60 > 4.32$, I reject $H_0$. This means $X_3$ cannot be dropped—it provides significant additional predictive power beyond $X_1$ and $X_2$.

response.text:
# Solution to Multiple Regression Analysis

## Part (1): Global F-Test of H₀: β₁ = β₂ = β₃ = 0

**Hypotheses:**
- H₀: β₁ = β₂ = β₃ = 0
- Hₐ: At least one βⱼ ≠ 0

**Calculate residual sum of squares:**
$$SS(Residual) = SS(Total) - SSReg(X_1, X_2, X_3) = 248.0 - 181.8 = 66.2$$

**Compute F-statistic:**
$$F = \frac{SSReg(X_1, X_2, X_3)/p}{SS(Residual)/(n-p-1)} = \frac{181.8/3}{66.2/21} = \frac{60.6}{3.1524} \approx 19.21$$

**Critical value:** $F_{0.05}(3, 21) \approx 3.07$

**Conclusion:** Since F = 19.21 > 3.07, **reject H₀**. There is highly significant evidence that at least one predictor is useful in predicting Y.

---

## Part (2): Extra SSReg(X₃ | X₁, X₂)

The partial (or sequential) regression sum of squares for X₃ given X₁ and X₂ is:

$$SSReg(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2) = SSReg(X_1, X_2, X_3) - SSReg(X_1, X_2)$$
$$= 181.8 - 145.2 = \boxed{36.6}$$

This represents the additional variation in Y explained by X₃ after X₁ and X₂ are already in the model.

---

## Part (3): Test Whether X₃ Can Be Dropped

**Hypotheses:**
- H₀: β₃ = 0 (X₃ is not needed)
- Hₐ: β₃ ≠ 0 (X₃ is needed)

**Compute F-statistic:**
$$F = \frac{SSReg(X_3 \mid X_1, X_2)/1}{MS(Residual)} = \frac{36.6}{66.2/21} = \frac{36.6}{3.1524} \approx 11.60$$

**Critical value:** $F_{0.05}(1, 21) \approx 4.32$

**Conclusion:** Since F = 11.60 > 4.32, **reject H₀**. X₃ **cannot be dropped**; it provides statistically significant additional explanatory power beyond X₁ and X₂.

---

## Part (4): First Row of Reduced-Model X-Matrix for Testing H₀: β₂ = β₃ = 0

**Reduced model:** Testing H₀: β₂ = β₃ = 0 means retaining only X₁ (and the intercept).

The reduced model is: $Y = β_0 + β_1X_1 + ε$

**X-matrix for reduced model:** n × 2 matrix with columns [1, X₁]

**First row of reduced-model X-matrix:**
$$\boxed{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1985 \end{bmatrix}}$$

Or in augmented form (if including the response):
$$\boxed{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1985 \\ \end{bmatrix}} \quad \text{with} \quad Y_1 = 10$$

The first row contains the intercept column (1) and the value of X₁ = 1985 for the first observation.
